morph.note: Imperative second singular of a thematic root: the bare stem, with no ending. Doubled (गर्ज गर्ज) it is a taunt — ‘go on, roar!’.
Simple future of √गर्ज् with the connecting vowel इ (-इष्य-). The same verb as the taunt: his roaring now, theirs soon.
Locative absolute (सति सप्तमी): मया त्वयि हते ‘you having been slain by me’, i.e. ‘once I have killed you’. The agent of the participle stands in the instrumental.
Present of √पा ‘to drink’ on the substitute stem पिब- (the perfect is पपौ, 3.34). After यावत् the present marks the action that runs alongside: ‘while I drink’.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) मूढ, यावत् अहं मधु पिबामि, (तावत्) क्षणं गर्ज गर्ज। मया त्वयि हते (सति) अत्र एव देवताः आशु गर्जिष्यन्ति।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: an imperative with a time clause (यावत् … with the correlative तावत् understood), then a future with a locative absolute.
mantras.lit: Roar, roar for a moment, O fool, while I drink the wine. When you have been slain by me, the gods will soon roar right here.
mantras.tr: Roar, fool, roar on for a moment, while I drink this wine. When I have slain you, it is the gods who will be roaring here — and soon.
mantras.tr_note: The second ‘roar’ is the gods’ shout of triumph; ‘it is the gods who’ brings out the contrast the repeated verb makes.

comm.t: The Goddess’s only speech in the chapter, and a taunt. The same verb, √गर्ज्, carries both halves: his roaring lasts a moment (क्षणम्), the gods’ roaring will follow his death on this very spot (अत्रैव). She names the drink मधु; the narrator called it ‘the supreme drink’ (3.34).
In recitation the line is among the best known of the Devī Māhātmya. The tradition hears in it the Goddess’s complete assurance: the outcome is already decided while she drinks.
A modern reading: arrogance is loud and brief. The verse gives it its moment — क्षणम् — and does not answer it in kind.

ā + ā → ā. The Gita Press writes a double avagraha (ऽऽ) to show that a long ā has been absorbed, so that सा and आरूढा can be told apart; it is a reading aid, not a sound.

morph.note: Past participle of आ + √रुह् (h + t → ḍh, with the vowel lengthened: रूढ). With √रुह् the participle may be active and take an object: तं महासुरम् आरूढा ‘she mounted the great asura’.
Absolutive with -य because the root carries prefixes (सम् + उद्): ‘having leapt up’.
एनद् is an unaccented pronoun used only for someone already in view (anvādeśa); it never begins a sentence.
Imperfect of the curādi root √तड् (stem ताडय-, with vṛddhi of a).

mantras.anvaya: एवम् उक्त्वा समुत्पत्य सा तं महासुरम् आरूढा (सती) पादेन कण्ठे आक्रम्य च शूलेन एनम् अताडयत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A chain of absolutives (उक्त्वा, समुत्पत्य, आक्रम्य) and a participle (आरूढा) leading to one finite verb, अताडयत्. कण्ठे is taken with आक्रम्य (‘pressing on the neck with her foot’); it can also go with अताडयत् (‘struck him on the neck’).
mantras.lit: Having spoken thus, leaping up, she mounted that great asura, and pressing (him) down on the neck with (her) foot, struck him with (her) spear.
mantras.tr: With these words she leapt up and mounted the great demon; pressing her foot on his neck, she struck him with her spear.

comm.t: Words become action at once. The Goddess’s foot on the buffalo’s neck and her spear in his body make the image the text is known for — the form painted and sculpted as Mahiṣāsuramardinī.

The weapon here is the शूल, which the Goddess received from Śiva (2.19–20 in the chapter of her arising). The foot on the asura’s neck is read in the tradition as total mastery: the enemy is held, not merely struck.

morph.note: Instrumental of the consonant stem पद् ‘foot’, which supplies the weak cases of पाद (पदा, पद्भ्याम् …). The Goddess’s foot was पादेन in 3.40.
निष्क्रान्त is the past participle of निस् + √क्रम् (s → ṣ after i, the root vowel lengthened before -त: क्रान्त).
Past participle of सम् + √वृ: ‘covered, enclosed’, hence ‘held, restrained’.

mantras.anvaya: ततः तया पदा आक्रान्तः सः अपि ततः निजमुखात् अर्धनिष्क्रान्तः एव आसीत्, देव्याः वीर्येण संवृतः (सन्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first ततः is ‘then’, the second ‘from there’ (from the buffalo body), defined by निजमुखात्. देव्याः may also be read as देव्या (instrumental, ‘by the Goddess’) with संवृतः; the spelling देव्या वीर्येण fits both.
mantras.lit: Then he too, pinned by her foot, from there, from his own mouth, had only half come out, held fast by the power of the Goddess.
mantras.tr: Pinned beneath her foot, the asura began to come forth from the buffalo’s mouth in his own form, but got only halfway, held fast by the Goddess’s power.
mantras.tr_note: ‘In his own form’ and ‘the buffalo’s mouth’ interpret निजमुखात् ततः: he emerges from the mouth of the body he is in. ‘Began to’ renders the sense of एव ‘only (half)’.

comm.t: The last transformation fails. Pinned by her foot, the asura tries to leave the buffalo body through its mouth and is caught halfway, held by the Goddess’s power.

This half-emerged figure — part buffalo, part warrior — is the moment shown in many images of Mahiṣāsuramardinī. The tradition reads it as the self caught between the forms it has taken and the one it is.

flags.uncertain: देव्या वीर्येण: genitive देव्याः (‘by the Goddess’s power’, chosen) or instrumental देव्या (‘by the Goddess, with her power’); the printed text allows both.
